options: Disappears lying down or with gentle pressure
Appears only on standing or straining
Vomiting since the lump became painful
Distension with no stool or flatus

history.ask: Any wound, ulcer, or infection in the leg, foot, or genitalia
Fever, night sweats, or weight loss
Varicose veins in the same leg
Back pain or known spine disease (including TB)

red_flags: Tense, tender, irreducible lump with vomiting — strangulated hernia; urgent surgical referral
Sudden pain in a previously reducible lump that no longer reduces — incarceration on its way to strangulation; urgent surgical referral
Redness of the skin over the lump with fever — strangulation with sepsis or an abscess
Distension with absolute constipation and a groin lump — obstructed hernia, and a femoral hernia is the classic missed cause
Small tender lump below the groin crease in an elderly woman with vomiting — femoral hernia strangulates early and looks trivial
exam: Examine standing first, then lying — hernias and saphena varix often vanish supine
Ask the patient to cough and look and feel for an expansile impulse
Test reducibility gently — direction of reduction helps type the hernia; never force a tender lump
Locate the lump against the pubic tubercle — above and medial (inguinal) vs below and lateral (femoral)
Examine the scrotum: can you get above the swelling? A lump you cannot get above is inguinoscrotal
Percuss and auscultate the lump — resonance or bowel sounds mean bowel content
Feel for a fluid thrill on tapping the saphenous vein below and a disappearance on lying — saphena varix; check the same leg for varicosities
Palpate for expansile pulsation — femoral artery aneurysm sits exactly where a femoral hernia does
Palpate the other groin and both hernial orifices — bilateral disease is common
Examine the leg, perineum, and genitalia for a septic source when nodes are suspected, and feel the node group's consistency and matting
Extend the hip against resistance (psoas stretch) and examine the spine when a deep tender swelling with back pain suggests psoas abscess

investigations.why: First-line discriminator: shows a hernial sac with cough impulse vs solid lymph node vs vascular structure (varix, aneurysm) vs cord lipoma when the exam is equivocal
Leukocytosis supports strangulation or an abscess; lymphocytosis or cytopenias with rubbery nodes support lymphoma
Markedly raised supports TB (psoas abscess, tuberculous nodes) or deep sepsis over an uncomplicated hernia

investigations.test: FNAC of a persistent lymph node
investigations.why: Separates reactive hyperplasia from tuberculous lymphadenitis and metastatic or lymphomatous nodes when no septic source is found
Air-fluid levels confirm obstruction when a hernia has stopped reducing and vomiting has begun
Second-line — if psoas abscess or an obscure obstructed hernia is suspected: defines the sac, its content, and any retroperitoneal collection or spinal focus
